title: How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina
text:
How Rizos Curls’ Julissa Prado Gets It All Done as a Multi-Hyphenate Latina

Sponsor Disclaimer: This article and accompanying podcast episode were sponsored by TextNow.

There’s no shortage of rules for how a Latina is supposed to live. Be ambitious, pero no te pases. Make your family proud, but don’t take up too much space. Work hard, but don’t make anyone uncomfortable by wanting more. And if you dare to question any of it? Well, you might just be called “una sinvergüenza.” Sound familiar?

For too long, that word has been used as a shaming tactic to silence us and put us in our so-called place. But what if we reclaim it? To me, being a sinvergüenza is being a woman without shame — living fully, taking up space, speaking our truth, and reclaiming the parts of ourselves we’ve been told to hide. And aren’t we deserving of that? I think so.

That’s why Somos launched Sin Vergüenza, a biweekly podcast for young Latinas who are figuring out how to live their best, most authentic lives, even when the world around us feels anything but easy. Each episode tackles the questions and challenges that come with being a multidimensional Latina today, from mental health, colorism, and dating to career negotiations, buying your first home, and everything in between. We’re bringing in Latina experts who get it to offer the insight, honesty, and guidance we don’t always have access to.

And we’re kicking things off with a conversation we know many of you will resonate with: How the hell are we supposed to get everything done?

According to a 2026 study from the Latino Donor Collaborative and Kantar, 61% of Latinas have multiple streams of income. Whether it’s because of economic uncertainty or a changing work culture, more of us are juggling multiple jobs, side projects, and personal brands. And not all of us are pulling it off. At least, not without burning ourselves out. For some, it’s the pressure to end generational poverty for ourselves and our loved ones. For others, it’s about making room for all the professional and creative parts of ourselves that we refuse to fit into a single box.

Whatever the reason, the work — and the to-do list — keeps piling up. So how do we actually do it all without completely running ourselves into the ground? Enter Julissa Prado. As the founder of Rizos Curls, the self-funded, multimillion-dollar haircare brand rooted in culture and community, Prado knows what it means to build something meaningful while balancing all the other pieces of her life. In our first episode of Sin Vergüenza, she gets real about how she manages it all and why doing more doesn’t necessarily mean doing everything at once.

Prado shares the strategies, patience, boundaries, and yes, self-love that have helped her grow Rizos Curls while making space for herself along the way. From a grading system that helps her prioritize the items on her to-do list to only putting on her plate what she’d serve her own figurative daughter, she offers advice for anyone trying to build a career, pursue a dream, care for the people they love, and still have something left for themselves at the end of the day.

Welcome to Sin Vergüenza, where young Latinas come to figure life out without shame, judgment, or the pressure to have it all together.

title: The Silence At The 2026 Emmys Spoke Volumes — Whiter, Quieter & Way Too Comfortable
text:
The Silence At The 2026 Emmys Spoke Volumes — Whiter, Quieter & Way Too Comfortable

For the first time in five years, no actor of color won a major acting Emmy during the primetime broadcast. It’s an awkward fact to sit with after a night of speeches about the importance of storytelling, artistic communities, and television’s allegedly limitless capacity to reflect the world back at us. The winners were talented, but that’s not the point. For an industry that has spent years promising audiences it is finally serious about representation, the 2026 Emmys delivered a familiar image: a parade of white acting winners accepting trophies while actors of color watched from their tables.

And yes, I understand the Emmys are an awards show. It’s built around expensive gowns, nervous clapping and television stars pretending they didn’t rehearse their acceptance speeches in the mirror. But awards matter. No matter how much glitter you throw at it, art will always be political. The same goes for the award shows celebrating it. They shape whose work gets remembered, whose career gets a jetpack and what kinds of stories studios decide are worth funding next time around.

This year’s result followed the least diverse Emmy nominations slate in a decade. By the end of the main telecast, the major acting honours had gone to Noah Wyle, Rhea Seehorn, Jean Smart, Matthew Rhys, Kate O’Flynn and Stephen Root. One thing they all had in common was that they were white. It was a rough outcome for a field that included performers such as Sterling K. Brown, Zendaya, Quinta Brunson, Ayo Edebiri, Janelle James, Yahya Abdul-Mateen II and Chase Infiniti.

The night was not entirely without politics, but it just felt oddly restrained considering the conditions surrounding it. Sally Field won the Emmy for Outstanding Lead Actress in a Limited or Anthology Series or Movie for Remarkably Bright Creatures and gave the sort of speech that made the room feel briefly connected to the actual world. The series was shot in Canada, which prompted Field to call the country “Blessed Canada! Our neighbours, our friends”. In another year, that might have simply been a location shout-out. Given the Trump administration’s trade dispute with Canada, it landed with rather more force (although still dancing on the line of palatable politics). Field continued, saying: “We’re the arts. We matter. Our voices matter. Our diversity, our unique storytelling, matters. We can’t let those voices be silenced or compromized or merged.”

The final word was doing some heavy lifting there, pointing to Paramount Skydance’s proposed $110 billion acquisition of Warner Bros. Discovery, which continues to hang over Hollywood. David Ellison runs Paramount Skydance, but the deal is backed in part by his father, Oracle co-founder Larry Ellison, who seems to be in a bromance with Donald Trump. The family’s links to the US president have attracted scrutiny, particularly because Trump has publicly said he would like CNN, currently owned by Warner Bros. Discovery, to end up in Paramount’s hands.

The deal is currently stalled by an antitrust challenge brought by a group of state attorneys general, led by California. If it proceeds, it would put major studios, streamers, cable brands, and news outlets under one corporate roof, meaning fewer companies and people would have a huge say over what gets made, who gets hired, and which stories reach an audience. That could have devastating consequences.

That backdrop made Stephen Colbert’s win for The Late Show feel a little heavier than the usual awards-show victory lap. CBS cancelled the program earlier this year, calling it “purely a financial decision”, and its final episode aired in May. Trump had made no secret of his contempt for Colbert or the show. When CBS announced the cancellation, he wrote on Truth Social that he “absolutely love[d] that Colbert got fired”, and later celebrated the final episode by calling Colbert “a total jerk”.

Colbert did not turn his Emmy acceptance speech into a long grievance session; instead, he spoke about the people whose jobs disappeared with the show. “The thing about these late shows is that, besides bringing a really good, steady job, is that they require so many people that they’re a fantastic incubator for young people to come in to learn to work professionally on a deadline in cooperation, in collaboration, and that is the future of our business that we have to look after,” he said.

That was the closest the Emmys got to reckoning with the people left exposed by an entertainment industry that keeps demanding fewer workers do more work, for less certainty, while executive suites pursue bigger deals. The Television Academy itself had already made that tension impossible to ignore. Before the ceremony, it moved five categories out of the primetime broadcast: supporting actor and actress in a limited or anthology series or movie, directing and writing for limited or anthology series or movies, and writing for a variety series. The Academy said it wanted “a fresh new take on the Emmys broadcast,” but SAG-AFTRA, the WGA, and the DGA criticized the move.

“The decision to eliminate these categories from the prime-time broadcast devalues the contributions of the talented people the Academy is meant to honour,” the guilds said in a joint statement. “An awards show dedicated to recognising excellence should not reduce recognition for the artists whose work gives it meaning.”

It’s hard to argue with that. Last year, the Emmys had a much more visible political current. Hannah Einbinder used her win to say “Fuck ICE” and call for a “Free Palestine”. Javier Bardem wore a keffiyeh and spoke against Israel’s genocide in Gaza, and several attendees wore Artists4Ceasefire pins. Television Academy chair Cris Abrego also used the stage to criticize Congress for voting to defund the Corporation for Public Broadcasting. Tramell Tillman made history as the first Black actor to win Outstanding Supporting Actor in a Drama Series.

This year Jean Smart made history by becoming the first woman to win an acting Emmy for every single season of a show’s run. However, this year there was also no comparable collective show of dissent from the stage or the red carpet, despite the genocide in Gaza continuing, the US media landscape becoming even more politically charged, and a major corporate takeover fight playing out in Hollywood’s backyard.

If I wanted to be generous, I’d say that absence doesn’t mean every winner owed viewers a geopolitical statement. People can accept an Emmy without becoming a full-time spokesperson for every injustice on Earth. But when the entertainment industry speaks so often about courage, community and the power of art, its biggest night can feel strangely hollow when so few people are willing to connect those ideas to the present tense.

Sally Field did. Alan Cumming did too, using his acceptance speech to say: “The time for talk is over. It is now time to vote, America.” There were flickers of urgency. Mostly though, the 2026 Emmys played it safe… and very white. And perhaps that is the clearest political statement of all.

From PEDESTRIAN.TV
